title: U.S. CFTC sets policies on event contract data, using crypto to check financial boxes
summary: The derivatives regulator issues a rule on data reporting for event contracts and new guidance for how crypto assets can be used to meet regulatory requirements.
content: The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission has established new policies regarding event contract data reporting. Additionally, the derivatives regulator has issued guidance on how crypto assets can be utilized by firms to meet their financial and regulatory compliance requirements. These measures aim to provide clearer oversight in the evolving digital asset and derivatives markets.

title: Ethereum Foundation doubles protocol security team ahead of overhaul
summary: The foundation said its next upgrade will be harder than the Merge, and the required pace of development will make it easier to ship bugs.
content: The Ethereum Foundation has doubled the size of its protocol security team in preparation for a major network overhaul. The organization stated that its upcoming upgrade will be more complex than the previous Merge event. Officials warned that the faster pace of development required for the transition increases the risk of shipping bugs.

title: CFTC staff say bitcoin, ether can count toward derivatives firms’ operating expenses
summary: Staff at the CFTC issued an advisory saying certain regulated firms may count crypto such as bitcoin and ether toward operating costs.
content: Staff at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission have issued an advisory stating that certain regulated derivatives firms may count cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ether toward their operating expenses. This guidance provides clarity for companies dealing in digital assets under the regulatory framework, allowing them to include approved virtual currencies as part of the financial resources required to cover day-to-day operational costs.

title: Solana Price Prediction 2030: Is $2,000 SOL Still on the Table After a 75% Crash?
summary: Key takeaways SOL trades near $73, roughly 75% below its January 2025 high of $294, and tracked Binance whale positioning leans bearish (about 20% longs) while around 79% of broader accounts are long. PumpGlass shows a $19.5 million short-liquidation cluster near $79.01 and long-liquidation clusters near $69.39 and $68.01. Solana has lost roughly 75% of its value since reaching an all-time high of $294 in January 2025. Large futures traders are leaning bearish, yet institutional analysts continue to see a future in which SOL trades at four digit prices. So, how realistic is a $2,000 Solana price prediction for 2030? At around $73, SOL is trading at a fraction of the price some of Wall Street’s most optimistic forecasts suggest it could eventually reach. But a steep discount to an analyst’s target does not necessarily make an asset cheap. NewsBTC examined liquidation heatmaps, whale positions, historical price action, network economics and institutional valuation models to understand where Solana stands today and what it could realistically be worth by the end of the decade. The findings paint a more complicated picture than either bulls or bears might expect. Solana Whales Are Betting Against the Crowd Perhaps the most interesting signal right now comes from the derivatives market. According to a November 23 snapshot from PumpGlass, only around 20% of the tracked Binance whale position value was allocated to longs. Meanwhile, approximately 79% of the broader trader accounts were positioned long. Although the two figures measure different aspects of market positioning, the divergence is striking. Large traders appear considerably less optimistic than the wider trading crowd. The average entry price of tracked whale shorts stood near $77.63, compared with $77.05 for whale longs. With SOL trading around $73 at the time of observation, the short side was better positioned. Binance whale and trader positioning for SOL. Source: PumpGlass, November 23, 2026. The on-chain picture offers another reason for caution. On November 19, blockchain tracker Lookonchain reported that two large holders had unstaked a combined 2.31 million SOL worth approximately $169.4 million before transferring the tokens to Coinbase Prime-associated addresses. Exchange deposits do not necessarily mean those tokens were sold. Institutional investors use custody platforms for several purposes, including collateral management and portfolio rebalancing. Still, the movement is worth monitoring. What matters now is whether large holders begin accumulating again or whether the recent decline has further to run. Shorts accounted for roughly 72% of those liquidations. SOL had gained around 3.1% over the same rolling period. The recovery is consistent with some bearish positions being forced out of the market. However, a liquidated short is not the same as a new investor buying SOL for the next four years. Until stronger spot demand emerges, traders should be careful about interpreting a short squeeze as the beginning of a sustainable recovery. Liquidation concentrations are modeled estimates, not guaranteed future orders, and can change considerably as traders adjust their positions. Solana Technical Analysis: The Levels That Could Change Everything Solana’s price structure has deteriorated considerably since its September recovery. After closing July near $72.79, SOL climbed to $103 in August and $117.99 in September. The recovery subsequently unraveled, with October closing near $95.35 before prices returned to the low $70s in November. Solana (SOL) price chart, 2026. Source: Binance SOLUSDT, TradingView. Looking at SOL’s historical price action on Binance, using the TradingView SOLUSDT market as the chart reference, five key price regions stand out: SOL price Technical significance $60–$65 Major downside reference $69–$71 Immediate support $75–$80 short term resistance $88–$95 Intermediate recovery zone $100–$118 Broader trend recovery territory The daily Relative Strength Index was in the low 30s in the observed CoinGlass data, suggesting weak momentum and proximity to oversold territory. But oversold markets can remain oversold. A sustained recovery above $80 would be the first encouraging development. Reclaiming $95 and subsequently $100 would provide stronger evidence that buyers are regaining control. On the downside, failure to hold the $65 range would bring Solana’s 2026 low near $60.42 back into focus. Our technical assessment remains cautious. There is room for a meaningful relief rally, particularly given the nearby short-liquidation exposure, but the broader market structure has yet to establish a convincing reversal. The $73 Token Behind a Multibillion-Dollar Economy While Solana’s price has struggled, its blockchain continues to facilitate substantial financial activity. According to DefiLlama, Solana’s November 23 network metrics included: Network metric Reported value DeFi total value locked $4.68 billion Stablecoin market capitalization $13.14 billion Daily DEX trading volume $1.12 billion Daily active addresses 1.8 million Daily transactions 83.42 million Daily application revenue $2.07 million Daily chain revenue $23,978 There is something particularly interesting about those last two figures. Applications running on Solana generated considerably more revenue than the chain itself under DefiLlama’s respective measurement definitions. This highlights what could become Solana’s biggest valuation challenge. A blockchain can attract substantial activity and billions of dollars in trading volume without its native token capturing a proportional share of that economic value. Cheap transactions are excellent for adoption. Whether they are equally good for SOL’s valuation is another question entirely. That is why Solana’s expansion beyond speculative trading could prove so important. The blockchain’s growing presence in stablecoins, payments and tokenized real-world assets opens the door to financial activity that could persist even when speculative markets cool. Its infrastructure is also evolving. The Solana Foundation reported the activation of Alpenglow in October 2026, targeting transaction finality near 150 milliseconds. November’s introduction of Solana 1.0 marked another milestone in the network’s development. Meanwhile, the announced integration with DTCC’s Tokenization Service, expected in the second half of 2027, could represent a meaningful institutional opportunity. The real test will be how much financial activity these developments ultimately bring onchain, and how much value SOL captures from it. The $1.38 Trillion Problem With a $2,000 Solana Here is something many price predictions overlook: Solana’s token supply will not necessarily remain where it is today. Unlike Bitcoin, SOL has no fixed maximum supply. Its inflationary issuance framework rewards validators and staking participants, while future governance decisions can influence the rate of supply growth. With around 592 million SOL currently circulating, we use an illustrative assumption of 690 million total tokens by 2030 for our valuation scenarios. Outcomes outside these ranges, including substantially greater losses, are possible. Bearish Scenario: $40–$110 Solana remains relevant but struggles to turn network adoption into meaningful economic value for SOL. Institutional projects develop more slowly than expected, competitors gain market share, and speculative trading remains an important source of demand. Solana does not need to fail for this scenario to materialize. It only needs to fall short of the expectations investors have placed on it. Base Scenario: $180–$400 Our central expectation assumes Solana retains its position among the leading smart-contract networks while expanding its role in payments, DeFi and tokenized financial assets. Under this scenario, the network does not need to dominate global finance. It needs to establish a durable position within it and capture more economic value from the applications it supports. Bullish Scenario: $600–$1,000 Solana becomes a major platform for tokenized equities, stablecoin settlements and high-frequency financial applications. Institutional adoption moves beyond announcements, network revenue expands significantly, and the broader cryptocurrency market benefits from favorable liquidity conditions. At $1,000, SOL would trade at approximately 13.8 times its November 23 reference price. Extreme Scenario: $1,500–$2,000+ This is where the most ambitious institutional predictions become conceivable. Solana would need to capture a significant share of a much larger on-chain financial economy, scale its infrastructure accordingly, and translate that activity into sustained demand for SOL. An exceptional cryptocurrency bull market could also temporarily push valuations beyond what underlying economics justify. We would not consider this the most likely outcome based on today’s evidence. The Five Signals That Could Make Us Raise Our Forecast Rather than following every new price target, long-term SOL investors may benefit from monitoring five developments: Stablecoin adoption: Growth in recurring payment and settlement activity beyond speculative trading. Institutional tokenization: Actual financial instruments and trading volumes going live on Solana. Network economics: Sustained growth in fees, economic value and demand for SOL. Institutional capital: Persistent ETF inflows and broader spot-market participation. Technical resilience: Reliable performance under heavy demand without sacrificing security or decentralization. Competition from Ethereum, its scaling ecosystem and specialized financial networks remains a considerable risk. If Solana’s transaction volumes rise while the economic value captured by the network stagnates, we would have reason to lower our valuation assumptions, regardless of how impressive the adoption statistics look. Is Solana Undervalued at $73? The current market offers an interesting contradiction. Solana’s blockchain has established a meaningful financial ecosystem, yet its token is trading roughly 75% below its historical record. Large futures traders are cautious, while institutional research continues to outline substantial long-term opportunities. Our $180 to $400 base-case range for 2030 reflects the possibility that Solana can grow without fulfilling every ambitious expectation placed on it. A move toward $1,000 is conceivable under considerably stronger conditions. At $2,000, however, investors would be betting on Solana becoming one of the world’s most valuable digital financial networks. The opportunity is there. The evidence that would justify such a valuation is not there yet. For now, the most interesting question surrounding Solana is not how many transactions it can process, but how much those transactions will eventually be worth to SOL holders. title: Bitcoin didn’t crash 70%, but Kraken’s order book did – Here’s what went wrong
summary: Kraken's BTC/CAD market's 70% price collapse has raised questions about market-maker liquidity and trading risks.

title: Binance Hack: US Moves to Recover $1.1 Billion, but Who Gets the Money?
summary: Key takeaways US authorities filed a civil forfeiture complaint on November 23 seeking more than $1.1 billion in USDC linked to the October 29 Binance hack, across 36 addresses on 18 blockchains. Circle froze the funds but says it cannot technically move them, so it proposes issuing replacement USDC to the US after a forfeiture order. Frozen is not recovered: the filings advance the legal-control stage, while final distribution and ownership remain undecided. A separate Abu Dhabi court order adds a second jurisdiction, and Circle’s reserve and supply reporting for the replacement tokens will deserve scrutiny. Nearly four weeks after the Binance hack, US authorities have filed a civil forfeiture complaint seeking more than $1.1 billion in USDC linked to the October theft. The money is already subject to restrictions, but the latest court filings reveal a complication: freezing stolen cryptocurrency is considerably easier than returning it. The complaint, filed on November 23, in the US District Court for the District of Columbia, targets USDC associated with 36 cryptocurrency addresses across 18 blockchains. Federal investigators attribute the October 29 attack to North Korean hacking groups, including the Lazarus Group. The complaint puts the value of the original theft at approximately $6 billion. For Binance, the latest legal action represents another opportunity to recover a portion of its losses. For the wider cryptocurrency industry, however, the case raises questions about the authority stablecoin issuers exercise over digital assets and what happens when governments become involved. Binance Hack Recovery Enters a New Legal Phase The assets targeted by US authorities are not an entirely new discovery. Earlier this month, NewsBTC reported that Circle had frozen approximately $1.1 billion in USDC linked to the Binance hack, following cooperation with law enforcement. What has changed is the government’s attempt to establish a legal basis for taking possession of those assets. According to the court documents, US authorities obtained a temporary restraining order on November 12. Prosecutors subsequently requested that the restrictions remain in place throughout the civil forfeiture proceedings. Both Binance and Circle consented to the initial restraining order and the requested extension, according to the government’s November 23 application. The agreement between the companies and federal authorities reduces one immediate obstacle to preserving the funds. It does not, however, resolve the question of their ultimate ownership or distribution. Civil forfeiture proceedings are directed against property believed to be connected to criminal activity. Interested parties can assert legitimate claims to that property through the legal process. In this case, prosecutors are seeking forfeiture of the assets to the United States. That is not the same thing as a court ordering their immediate return to Binance. Circle Cannot Simply Send the Frozen USDC Back Perhaps the most interesting disclosure in the complaint concerns Circle itself. The stablecoin issuer can restrict transfers involving USDC held at particular blockchain addresses. However, that authority does not necessarily give Circle direct control over the wallets holding those tokens. The complaint states that Circle: “ does not have the technical ability to transfer the Defendant Property from the blocklisted Subject Addresses to the United States US forfeiture complaint · November 23 filing Instead, Circle has agreed to issue an equivalent amount of replacement USDC and transfer those tokens to US authorities upon receiving a forfeiture order from the court. The proposed arrangement exposes an unusual feature of centralized stablecoins. An issuer can prevent tokens from circulating without possessing the private keys needed to move them. It also raises an accounting question that deserves attention. If replacement tokens are issued, what ultimately happens to the original frozen USDC, and how will Circle ensure that the treatment of those balances is reflected accurately in its outstanding supply and reserve reporting? The issuance of replacement tokens would not, by itself, prove that USDC had become undercollateralized. Nevertheless, transparency around the implementation would be important for a stablecoin whose credibility depends on confidence in its backing. The immediate concern is not whether Circle can create new tokens. It is whether the entire recovery process can be independently accounted for. The $1.1 Billion Is Not Back With Binance Yet The temptation to describe the Justice Department’s announcement as a billion-dollar recovery is understandable. It is also premature. There are three separate stages involved: restricting access to the stolen assets, obtaining legal authority over them and determining how they will ultimately be distributed. The November 23 filings advance the second stage. They do not establish that the third has been completed. The $1.1 billion Binance recovery process. Source: US District Court for the District of Columbia filings, November 23, 2026. There is also a cross-border complication. On November 18, Reuters reported that an Abu Dhabi court had directed several cryptocurrency companies, including Circle, to preserve digital assets associated with the Binance theft. The involvement of authorities in both the United States and the United Arab Emirates illustrates how a single cryptocurrency theft can generate legal proceedings across multiple jurisdictions. Blockchain transactions may cross national borders without much difficulty. Establishing ownership rights over the assets involved is a considerably less straightforward exercise. That does not mean the US and UAE proceedings are necessarily in conflict. But the ultimate disposition of the funds will require more than an announcement from either government. For investors assessing Binance’s financial position, the distinction between frozen assets and recovered capital is particularly important. Restricted cryptocurrency should not automatically be treated as money already returned to the exchange. The Binance Hack Tests the Case for Centralized Stablecoins For years, the ability of stablecoin issuers to freeze tokens has been criticized by advocates of decentralized finance. The Binance case demonstrates the other side of that argument. Without Circle’s ability to restrict transactions, preserving such a large amount of cryptocurrency for potential recovery would have been more difficult. In this particular case, centralized control has provided a mechanism that may help prevent suspected criminals from benefiting from stolen assets. The uncomfortable question is whether the cryptocurrency industry can benefit from that authority while also demanding meaningful safeguards against its misuse. The answer depends partly on transparency. Token holders should be able to understand why assets were frozen, under what legal authority restrictions remain in place and how disputes over ownership are resolved. The same standard should apply to the exchange, the stablecoin issuer and the government. The next significant development in the Binance case will be the court’s treatment of the forfeiture claim and any competing claims to the assets. Circle’s proposed issuance of replacement USDC will also deserve scrutiny if it proceeds. Until then, the $1.1 billion should be understood as assets subject to an ongoing recovery effort, not a completed repayment. For a cryptocurrency industry that frequently celebrates the speed of moving money, the Binance hack is a reminder that getting it back can be an entirely different business.
content: US authorities have filed a civil forfeiture complaint seeking over $1.1 billion in USDC linked to the recent Binance hack. While stablecoin issuer Circle previously froze the funds, it cannot technically move them and proposes issuing replacement tokens upon a final court order. The case highlights cross-border legal complexities and the ongoing debate over centralized control in the cryptocurrency industry.

content_ta: Oxford-ல் நடத்தப்பட்ட ஒரு ஆய்வில், AI agents-கள் குறைபாடுள்ள பணிகளை மதிப்பாய்வு செய்பவர்களை ஏமாற்றி ஒப்புதல் பெற முடியும் என்பது கண்டறியப்பட்டுள்ளது. இந்த கண்டுபிடிப்பு கல்வி ஒருமைப்பாடு மற்றும் AI-உதவி மதிப்பீடுகளின் நம்பகத்தன்மைக்கு குறிப்பிடத்தக்க ஆபத்துக்களை ஏற்படுத்துகிறது.
